AI-Led Transactions Must Verify Human Authorization, FIDO CEO Says
articles.description: “For a future in which artificial intelligence (AI) agents log in and conduct transactions on behalf of people to become a reality, we need to be able to prove that a real person is behind those actions. We must be able to verify whether a person is conducting a transaction directly or has delegated authority to an AI agent, and control the scope of that authority. Establishing this foundation of trust is essential for AI agents to operate safely.” Andrew Shikiar, CEO of the FIDO Alliance, emphasized the need for new authentication and security frameworks in the age of AI agents during his keynote address at Authenticate U.S. 2026, held in Carlsbad, California, on October 19 (local time). Andrew Shikiar, CEO of the FIDO Alliance, delivers a keynote address at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. Authenticate is a digital identity and authentication conference organized by the FIDO Alliance, an international organization that develops online authentication standards. The seventh annual U.S. conference was held from October 19 to 21 under the theme “New Frontiers,” covering digital identity credentials and AI agent authentication alongside passkeys. During his keynote, Shikiar highlighted the growing adoption of passkeys, a passwordless authentication technology, while stressing that new security frameworks are needed as AI increasingly accesses services and conducts transactions on behalf of people. While traditional authentication has focused on preventing account takeovers and verifying legitimate users at login, future systems must also verify whether individual actions performed by AI agents have been authorized, he explained. AI Transactions Require Proof of Human Authorization For an AI agent to purchase products or conduct financial transactions on a user's behalf, it must be possible to verify that the agent has received authorization from the actual user and that the transaction falls within the permitted scope. Systems must also allow users to revoke delegated authority when necessary. Shikiar identified “Verified Human Identity” as a starting point for establishing such trust. The concept centers on the ability to verify that an AI agent's actions are grounded in the intentions of a real person. “Verified human identity does not mean that people have to disclose their identities to every service,” Shikiar explained. “Most services do not need to know exactly who a user is.” Instead, users should be able to prove that they are real people or meet specific eligibility requirements when necessary, without unnecessarily exposing personal information, he said. Shikiar also presented a hypothetical scenario set in 2030. A user asks an AI agent to find an apartment within a specified budget. The agent discovers an attractive property with a great view, but its price exceeds the authorized budget by 40%. In that situation, the AI agent cannot proceed with the application under its existing authority. It must obtain additional approval from the user. The example illustrates that delegating a task to AI does not give the agent unrestricted freedom to act. According to Shikiar, AI agents must respect the conditions established by users and disclose personal information only to the extent necessary for a transaction. The FIDO Alliance is developing specifications for AI agent payments to address these challenges. Building on technologies including Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) and Mastercard's Verifiable Intent, the organization is working on methods to verify human-delegated authority throughout the transaction process. At the conference, the alliance said it was preparing to release a working draft of the relevant specifications. A view of the keynote session at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California. / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. More Than 7 Billion Passkeys in Use as FIDO Expands Into Digital Identity The new security challenges posed by AI agents have emerged as passkey adoption continues to expand. According to Shikiar, more than 7 billion passkeys are estimated to be in use worldwide. He said passkeys, which began gaining widespread adoption in 2022, have become a major authentication method for online services within four years. The FIDO Alliance's 2026 Passkey Index also highlighted this progress. Based on data from 15 major global service providers, the index found that more than one-third of successful sign-ins were completed using passkeys. Passkey authentication was also approximately three times faster than traditional login methods. However, while passkeys reduce the risks of password theft and phishing, they do not independently verify a user's real-world identity or the authority delegated to an AI agent. The FIDO Alliance is therefore identifying digital identity credentials as a major priority beyond passkeys. Digital identity credentials allow people to electronically prove information such as their identity, age, educational background or professional qualifications. Instead of providing unnecessary personal information to a service, users can demonstrate that they meet specific requirements while preserving their privacy. In enterprise environments, such credentials can support remote employee onboarding, identity verification and account recovery. Shikiar stressed that widespread adoption will depend on interoperability among identity issuers, digital wallet providers and identity verifiers, even when they operate different systems. To support this goal, the FIDO Alliance is developing common certification requirements for digital wallets. At the conference, the organization also outlined plans to publish working drafts for Verifier ID, a mechanism for establishing whether an entity requesting personal information is legitimate, and the Credential Manager Reference Architecture (CMRA), a technical framework supporting digital wallet authentication. The alliance also announced plans to establish an external advisory forum to involve governments, identity issuers and other stakeholders in standards development. Its first meeting was scheduled for November 2026. Shikiar pointed to the adoption of standardized shipping containers, which significantly improved efficiency in the global logistics industry, as an example of the value of common standards. He argued that open standards and interoperability will be equally important for digital identity and AI-driven transactions. If companies rely on incompatible authentication systems, AI agents will struggle to conduct secure transactions across multiple services. “This foundation of trust must be open, standardized and interoperable,” Shikiar said. He expressed hope that, by 2030, the industry would be able to look back on its current efforts as having helped build a safer, more convenient and more productive internet. jk2@chosunbiz.com

articles.description: The Human Shelter: Expedition into What Makes a Home is an exploration of the feeling of home. Directed by Boris Bertram and funded by IKEA, the film looks at present ways of living in Norway, Iraq, the United States, Nigeria, Japan, Uganda, and Iceland, interrogating the role of home in order to project it into the future. Through imagery and personal narratives, the documentary connects the concept of home with landscape, movement and settling, time, migration and security, vulnerability, and nature. How do displaced populations create a home? When does a shelter become a home? Portraits, stories, and shelters across four continents give viewers a glimpse of an answer to these big questions in a one-hour film tour.

articles.title: Reproduce a Provably Fair Result with HMAC-SHA256
articles.description: A “provably fair” label becomes useful when you can turn it into a reproducible check. For a developer, the interesting part is the path from a previously published commitment to an exact game result: hash the revealed input, rebuild the HMAC message, then apply the documented byte conversion. That path has several distinct failure points. Getting the cryptography right is necessary, but the result also depends on the nonce, message format and game formula. A matching digest with the wrong result mapping is an incomplete verification. The walkthrough below uses example seeds created for the original CryptoPlay Guide article. They are not records of a casino bet. The Dice and Limbo mappings follow the published formulas described in that article; another operator may use different rules. Treat the commitment as your starting input Before betting, the operator shows a SHA-256 hash of a secret server seed. Save that hash. The client seed is visible, as is the nonce that identifies the bet within the seed pair. The operator reveals the old server seed after you rotate seeds. You therefore need the revealed server seed, the hash saved before play, the client seed and the exact nonce. You cannot complete this check while the active server seed remains secret. Here is the example server seed: cryptoplayguide-example-server-seed-2026 The pre-bet commitment for this example is: ea1e9ffa82b568d4ecb93488031e79bfe0cba227dbbe2b134c73e66079e78e91 Use this command to check it: printf %s "cryptoplayguide-example-server-seed-2026" | sha256sum Compare the entire output hash with the saved commitment. A mismatch means the revealed seed does not match that commitment; the later result calculation cannot repair that failed check. Preserve the input exactly. A trailing newline or space changes the hash, which is why the example uses printf %s rather than echo. Rebuild the HMAC message explicitly For this Dice and Limbo example, the server seed is the HMAC-SHA256 key. The message has the format client_seed:nonce:round, with round set to 0. Using client seed my-client-seed and nonce 1, the command is: printf %s "my-client-seed:1:0" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "cryptoplayguide-example-server-seed-2026" It produces: d6e37d4cd754f8752a46ef3f8c7bcd60434a1abe8a9ab09594833e9b21883b86 The placement of each input matters. Do not swap the key and message or silently change the message separators. Likewise, copy the nonce from the bet record: some operators start counting at 0, while others start at 1. At this stage you have reproduced the digest. You still need to reproduce the game result. Follow the byte mapping, then the payout mapping Take the first four bytes of the digest: d6 e3 7d 4c Those bytes are 214, 227, 125 and 76. Convert them as follows: 214/256 + 227/256² + 125/256³ + 76/256⁴ = 0.83940871… For Dice, apply: floor(value × 10001) / 100 The example result is 83.94. For Limbo with the example's 1% edge, apply: max(1, floor(0.99 / value × 100) / 100) The corresponding result is 1.17×. These are different mappings from the same underlying value. Copying a Dice conversion into a different game does not establish that game's result. For another useful check, keep the seeds and change the nonce to 2. The message becomes my-client-seed:2:0; the digest begins ad06e622, the value is 0.67588652…, and the Dice result is 67.59. Inspect the implementation without confusing game models The open-source verifier is available at: https://github.com/cryptoplayguide/provably-fair-verifier Its README describes a dependency-free JavaScript module for browsers or Node.js 18+ using the Web Crypto API. It checks commitments and implements the documented Dice and Limbo mappings. Its Limbo implementation rejects a float of zero, or a value outside (0, 1), with a RangeError rather than returning Infinity. The repository also supports a Crash model, but its inputs and byte handling differ: salt is the HMAC key, the game hash is the message, and the calculation takes the first 52 bits. That distinction is a reason to read the operator's fairness documentation before choosing a verifier mode. A browser interface is available at https://cryptoplay.guide/tools/provably-fair-verifier/. CryptoPlay Guide states that verification runs locally in the browser and sends nothing to CryptoPlay Guide. You can first reproduce the example, then use your own revealed inputs. Keep the conclusion narrow A successful check establishes that the supplied result matches the committed seed under the formula you used. It does not establish solvency, withdrawal reliability, licensing or an attractive house edge. Keep result verification and payout analysis as separate checks. Reproducing a roll explains where that roll came from; it does not make a negative expected return disappear. Originally published at https://cryptoplay.guide/guides/verify-provably-fair-step-by-step/ CryptoPlay Guide, the site this was originally published on, earns affiliate commissions from some casinos it covers. This post contains no affiliate links. 18+ (or the higher legal age where you live). Gambling involves risk of loss; only play where legal, set deposit, loss and time limits, and seek help if gambling causes harm, for example from BeGambleAware.org.

articles.title: After Passkeys, FIDO Turns to Digital Identity and AI Transaction Authentication
articles.description: The FIDO (Fast IDentity Online) Alliance, an international organization that develops online authentication standards, has identified digital identity verification and authorization for artificial intelligence (AI) agent transactions as its next major priorities following the widespread adoption of passkeys. As AI agents increasingly conduct transactions on behalf of people, common standards are needed to verify the scope of authority granted by users and determine who should be held responsible when problems arise. The FIDO Alliance outlined these priorities during the closing keynotes of Authenticate U.S. 2026, its annual authentication technology conference, held in Carlsbad, California, on October 21 (local time). Andrew Shikiar, CEO of the FIDO Alliance, at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California. / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. The three-day event, held from October 19 to 21 under the theme “New Frontiers,” explored the growing adoption of passkeys and developments in digital identity, payments and AI agent authentication. The final day's program featured presentations by Mastercard and the FIDO Alliance, followed by a panel discussion involving representatives from Visa, PayPal and other payment industry organizations. “Passkeys have shown what this industry can achieve when we align on a common vision, standards, certification and a consistent user experience,” said Andrew Shikiar, CEO of the FIDO Alliance. “Now we need to do the same for digital credentials.” Mastercard Highlights Passkey Success, New Authentication Needs for AI Purchases Jonathan Grossar, Senior Vice President at Mastercard, said passkeys are improving both security and convenience in online payments. According to Mastercard, authentication completion rates among consumers who have already enrolled payment passkeys exceed 95%. Jonathan Grossar, Senior Vice President at Mastercard, at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California. / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. By allowing customers to approve payments using fingerprint or facial authentication, much like unlocking a smartphone, passkeys reduce the inconvenience of entering passwords or switching to banking apps. Mastercard also presented Digital Payment Credentials (DPC) as a next step in payment authentication. Under the proposed approach, payment credentials issued by banks or other institutions would be stored in smartphone wallets. Consumers could review transaction details, including the amount and merchant, before approving payments through biometric authentication. Mastercard was testing related prototypes, while some features remained under development as part of ongoing standardization efforts. Authentication requirements become more complex when AI agents purchase products on behalf of consumers. Grossar described a scenario in which a consumer instructs an AI agent to purchase a T-shirt from a particular brand for less than $100. If the agent later finds a suitable product and completes the purchase, the payment system must be able to verify that the transaction was authorized, even though the consumer is not present at checkout. To address this challenge, Grossar introduced Verifiable Intent, a technology designed to connect a user's identity, purchase instructions and the actions subsequently taken by an AI agent. “We now need to prove not only that a transaction was authorized, but also that what the agent did was consistent with what the user intended,” Grossar said. Mastercard is working with the FIDO Alliance on related standardization efforts. EMVCo, a technical standards organization involving major international payment networks including Visa and Mastercard, is also developing common specifications for AI-driven payments. FIDO Alliance: “Trust Is Not a Feature, It Is an Outcome” Nishant Kaushik, Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of the FIDO Alliance, warned that technically secure authentication does not necessarily guarantee a trustworthy service. “Trust is not a feature. It is an outcome,” Kaushik said. Nishant Kaushik, CTO of the FIDO Alliance, at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California. / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. He explained that even when passkeys or digital wallets function correctly, users may still experience unfavorable outcomes. One example is an AI agent that authenticates successfully but takes actions the user did not intend or authorize. Kaushik also highlighted new risks that can emerge as authentication becomes easier. Passkeys have made it possible to combine secure login with a convenient user experience. However, easier identity verification could encourage businesses to request personal information more frequently and in situations where it may not be necessary. If users must disclose personal information to access essential services or avoid unfavorable conditions, their ability to provide meaningful consent may be limited. Kaushik argued that technical standards alone cannot resolve these challenges. Digital identity systems must also accommodate people with disabilities and users of older devices, while establishing clear accountability when incidents occur. He said digital identity infrastructure should become widely accessible, much like roads or telecommunications networks, emphasizing the need for cooperation among governments, businesses and standards organizations. Kaushik also urged the industry to evaluate authentication technologies by their real-world outcomes rather than adoption figures alone. “The measures should be whether actual fraud has decreased, whether users can access services more easily and whether unnecessary sharing of personal information has been reduced,” he said. Visa, PayPal and EMVCo Debate Responsibility for AI-Driven Purchases A panel discussion moderated by Dave Birch, a digital payments expert and co-founder of Consult Hyperion, examined the challenges that arise when AI agents make purchases on behalf of consumers. From left, Dave Birch, co-founder of Consult Hyperion; Gavin Shenker, Senior Director at Visa; Rakan Khalid, Senior Director at PayPal; and Arman Aygen, Senior Technical Director at EMVCo, during a panel discussion at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California. / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. Representatives from Visa and PayPal said AI agent transactions had begun to emerge, although transaction volumes remained relatively small. They nevertheless agreed that rapid technological development was creating an urgent need to define authorization boundaries and responsibility for transactions. Gavin Shenker, Senior Director at Visa, illustrated the problem with an example involving an AI agent instructed to purchase shoes. A consumer might specify a preferred color and price, but allowing the AI agent to accept nonrefundable purchase conditions raises a different question. Shenker said the industry needs ways for consumers to understand and approve relevant purchase terms without having to read lengthy terms and conditions for every transaction. Another challenge is determining how much personal information should be shared during AI-assisted purchases. Shenker noted that if a consumer asks an AI agent to organize a birthday party, a merchant selling birthday candles or a payment provider does not need to know the consumer's entire party plan. Payment systems should be able to verify that transactions have been properly authorized while disclosing only the information required by each participant. EMVCo is also examining technical frameworks for maintaining consistent authorization conditions throughout the purchasing process, from the consumer's initial instructions to final payment. Rakan Khalid, Senior Director at PayPal, emphasized buyer protection and responsibility for transaction disputes. If an AI agent purchases the wrong product or completes a payment the consumer did not authorize, existing refund and dispute resolution systems will need clear rules for evaluating what happened. Khalid said consumers, merchants and payment providers must be able to establish their respective responsibilities when an AI agent is involved in a transaction. Arman Aygen, Senior Technical Director at EMVCo, argued that AI payment standards should not focus solely on the final payment stage. Authorization conditions must be managed throughout the purchasing process, beginning when users instruct AI agents to search for and select products. He emphasized that cooperation among companies and standards organizations would be essential to establishing consistent technical requirements. Andrew Hindle, Chair of the Authenticate conference, at Authenticate U.S. 2026 in Carlsbad, California. / Photo by Jongkil Jeong. Following the public conference, the FIDO Alliance held a two-day Member Plenary on October 22 and 23 to continue technical and standardization discussions involving passkeys, digital credentials and AI agent payments. The meetings provided an opportunity for member companies and technical working groups to build on the issues raised during the three-day conference. In his closing remarks, Andrew Hindle, Chair of the Authenticate conference, highlighted the expanding scope of authentication technologies and the FIDO Alliance's work. “The scope of authentication is changing, and so is the scope of what FIDO addresses,” Hindle said. “To make the progress the industry needs, we need more people to get involved.” jk2@chosunbiz.com

articles.title: The console gathers dust, then deletes your games
articles.description: Sony's European PlayStation terms let the company close your account after 36 months of inactivity, and the terms say that closure is irreversible. Once the account is gone, so is access to every digital game bought through it. The clause has been in the terms for years. It drew fresh attention this weekend because Sony confirmed last week that from 2028, new PlayStation games will ship with no physical disc. The mechanism sits in two paragraphs of the European terms. Clause 21.2: "If you have not used your Account for at least 36 months we may take steps to close it. In that case, we will contact you via the email address registered to your Account and give you 6 months to either log in to your Account or contact us and tell us to keep your Account open." Clause 21.3: "After your Account is closed, you will not be able to access the PlayStation Online Services or use the Digital Products purchased with that Account. Account closure is irreversible." Anyone who has bought a game digitally through the PlayStation Store over the last 15 to 20 years has accepted these terms. Whether Sony actually runs that process is a separate question, and the sources do not show that it does. What is established is that the right exists on paper and the customer has agreed to it. Disc games are licensed too, and a license can in principle be revoked. A disc that holds the full game and needs no online activation cannot be pulled back in practice; a digital entitlement can be withdrawn whenever the platform decides. Sony has already demonstrated it will remove bought content from libraries, erasing 551 film titles that users had purchased. A popular theory this weekend tied the inactivity clause to GDPR, reasoning that the same wording does not appear in the US terms and GDPR took effect in May 2018. The dates do not support it. Videocardz traces the deletion policy back to at least 2009, when the window was 18 months. It grew to 24 months in 2016 and to 36 months in 2019. The policy predates GDPR and has moved on Sony's schedule, not a regulator's. Microsoft carries comparable inactivity terms that cover Xbox accounts, including in the US. Its version includes a carve-out: Microsoft commits not to delete accounts that hold digital purchases such as Xbox games. Sony offers no equivalent promise. The trigger is account activity, not any specific action, so a single login resets the clock. The six-month warning goes only to the registered email, so a stale address you no longer read is the realistic way to lose a library without noticing. If you keep a digital collection on a console that sits unused for years at a time, that collection now depends on you logging in often enough, or on future EU legislation forcing digital-ownership rights that do not exist today.

Malicious Downloads Can Hijack AI Coding Agents and Steal Tokens
articles.description: The attack exploits instruction files that AI coding tools use to understand project requirements. OpenAI Codex supports AGENTS.md, while Claude Code can read CLAUDE.md. These plain-text files typically contain legitimate guidance about coding standards, project setup and development workflows. However, an attacker can disguise harmful instructions as ordinary engineering documentation. When an AI agent opens the affected directory, it may interpret those instructions as trusted guidance and execute commands using its existing permissions. Forever securities discovered a malicious AGENTS.md file in a customer's Downloads folder that instructed Codex to install a suspicious npm package called function-color. The security system stopped the installation before the malware could execute. Although investigators could not establish how the original file reached the computer, they demonstrated that a malicious website could trigger a similar download without a separate approval prompt in certain browser configurations. OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Were Both Targeted Forever Security reproduced related attacks against two widely used AI coding assistants. In Codex experiments, the malicious instructions attempted to modify the agent's machine-wide configuration, register an external Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and install the malicious package. Because the configuration applied beyond the original working directory, the change could potentially affect subsequent sessions. Researchers reported that Codex followed the malicious instructions in more than 90% of their tests, most of which used a harmless substitute for the malware. The Claude Code demonstration used a different technique. A malicious CLAUDE.md file instructed the agent to redirect its API traffic to a researcher-controlled server. This could expose authentication tokens and allow the server to return instructions that the agent might execute. The configuration change succeeded in approximately half of the tests, according to the researchers. These results are specific to their experimental setups and have not been independently validated. Why This Attack Is Different From Traditional Malware Traditional malware typically relies on executable files, software vulnerabilities or users running malicious programs. This technique takes a different approach: it exploits the instructions an AI agent is designed to follow. The Markdown files themselves do not need to contain executable code. Instead, they persuade the agent to perform dangerous actions using its existing access to files, terminals, configuration settings and external services. This creates a significant security challenge. An AI assistant may be functioning as designed when it follows a project instruction, yet the instruction itself can be malicious. The risk increases when developers allow agents to run commands autonomously, access sensitive credentials or modify configuration files without independent approval. How Developers Can Protect Their AI Coding Agents Developers and organizations can reduce the risk by making a few changes to their workflows: Avoid running agents from Downloads: Start Codex, Claude Code and similar tools from the specific project directory they need to access. Review instruction files: Inspect unfamiliar AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and similar files before allowing an agent to follow them. Keep security controls enabled: Do not disable sandboxing, command approval prompts or other protective restrictions merely because an instruction file requests it. Check configuration changes: Review MCP server registrations, API endpoint settings and other machine-wide modifications that you did not authorize. Restrict package installations: Verify package names and sources, and use trusted registries or scanning tools before installing dependencies. Protect authentication tokens: Use isolated development environments, limit credential access and rotate potentially exposed tokens immediately. If a suspicious instruction file is discovered, developers should investigate whether the agent executed any commands or changed its configuration. If credentials may have been exposed, revoke or rotate them and review relevant account activity. A Growing Security Challenge for AI Development The incident highlights a broader issue as AI agents gain more autonomy. Their usefulness depends on reading documentation, interacting with tools and carrying out multi-step tasks, but those same capabilities can create opportunities for attackers. Security teams must therefore assess more than conventional executable malware. Project documentation, downloaded files, third-party packages and agent configuration settings can all influence what an AI assistant does. The safest approach is to separate instructions from permissions. An agent may read a file to understand a task, but that file should not be allowed to authorize changes to security controls or grant access to sensitive information. Final Thoughts Malicious downloads demonstrate how attackers can turn AI coding assistants into tools for compromising their own environments. By exploiting trusted instruction files, researchers showed how Codex and Claude Code could potentially be manipulated into installing malware, redirecting API traffic or exposing authentication credentials. The findings do not mean every AI coding session is vulnerable to successful exploitation, but they highlight the importance of secure working directories, reviewed instructions and restricted permissions. As AI-powered development becomes more common, keeping agents isolated, verifying dependencies and requiring approval for sensitive actions will be essential to protecting developers and their projects.

articles.title: "Creation without a creator": Pathologic 3's devs have refused to patch an invisible apple tree, and for a blissful moment, I thought they were lying to poison Google's AI
articles.description: Magnificent, depressing plague colony fable Pathologic 3 has received a sizeable game update that adds some new difficulty modes, a photo feature, and some new, worryingly folkloric methods of defeating a murky embodiment of disease. Developers Ice Pick Lodge have also staunchly refused to remove an invisible apple tree, describing this apparently "famous" bug as a hallmark of a game whose "symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product". This appears to be the last major update for Pathologic 3, so that invisible apple tree is staying in the game forever. I confess, when I first read the Steam blog in question, I doubted. The thing about invisible apple trees is that they are quite easy to confuse with apple trees that are simply not there. Pathologic in general is a house of lies: as Quintin Smith (RPS in peace) put it in his legendary Butchering Pathologic trilogy, "absolutely everybody has an angle, everyone's bending the truth and trying to twist you round their fingers." Pathologic 3 especially is a purgatorial time travel story that must be continually rewritten, a crock of festering rumours enclosed by an enormous, phantom theatre. As such, I read Ice-Pick's typically professorial account of the "invisible apple tree" with intense suspicion.

articles.title: AD—WO to Renovate the Heinz Architectural Center at Pittsburgh’s Carnegie Museum of Art
articles.description: Pittsburgh's Carnegie Museum of Art has commissioned architecture and urban design practice AD—WO to reimagine the Heinz Architectural Center. The practice, led by Emanuel Admassu and Jen Wood and one of the winners of the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards, was recognized for exploring relationships among people, place, history and material culture, bringing an interdisciplinary approach to the architecture experience. The Heinz Architectural Center is the museum's forum to present, explore and incubate architectural ideas, currently located in the institution's main building, which dates from 1907. The new design aims to transform the Center into a contemporary facility that brings together exhibitions, collections, research, learning and public engagement. AD—WO is working with R3A as architect of record, Buro Happold for engineering and sustainability, Tillotson Design Associates for lighting and VizzAcoustics for acoustics.

articles.title: Apple M6 for Developers: Local-First AI Is Now a Shipping Strategy, Not a Compromise
articles.description: Apple M6 for Developers: Local-First AI Is Now a Shipping Strategy, Not a Compromise Shivam Kumar · VisionQuantech · October 28, 2026 Apple's October 27, 2026 launch — a 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac on the new M6 chip — reads like a hardware story. For developers, it is an architecture story. The M6 MacBook Pro does AI work up to 25% faster than the M5 machine, the iMac up to 5x faster than the M4 machine, and the MacBook Pro claims up to 24 hours of battery life. The 14-inch Pro starts at $1,999, the iMac at $1,499, with pre-orders from October 28 and availability November 6. Those numbers redraw a decision developers have lived with for years: what runs on the device, and what has to go to the cloud? The decision that just changed Until now, the local-vs-cloud choice was a trade-off with a clear loser. Cloud models were strong but slow, metered, and privacy-expensive. Local models were private and instant but weak. The M6 generation narrows that gap from the device side at exactly the moment cloud models are getting cheaper from the other side. The practical result: a whole class of features — transcription, summarisation, document understanding, image work, code assistance — can now be designed local-first, with the cloud as a fallback for the hardest reasoning rather than the default for everything. That changes your cost model. A feature that runs on-device has no per-token bill, no inference server to scale, and no latency budget spent on a round trip. It also changes your privacy story: a tool that processes a client's documents or a patient's notes without uploading them is a fundamentally easier sell than one that ships data to a third party. Three things to build differently now 1. Design for always-on, not plugged-in. A 24-hour battery claim — Apple's best case, to be verified by reviewers — means background AI becomes feasible: a meeting assistant that listens all day, a research assistant that indexes as you work, a writing assistant that watches context instead of waiting to be asked. Build features that sip power and run continuously, not features that demand a charger. 2. Treat privacy as a feature, not a checkbox. If your product handles sensitive data, the M6 generation is your permission to build the local version first and market it as such. "Your data never leaves your Mac" is a line a cloud-only competitor cannot match. 3. Split the workload by tier, not by habit. Frontier reasoning still belongs in the cloud; everyday assistance belongs on the device. Route by task difficulty, not by what your architecture happened to do last year. The tiering discipline — cheap local for bulk, cloud flagship for the hardest 5% — is now the engineering skill that decides your margins. The caveat that keeps you honest These are Apple's claims, not independent benchmarks. The 25% and 5x figures, and the 24-hour battery number, need real-world verification across sustained workloads before you bet a roadmap on them. And $1,999 is a professional price — the local-first era arrives for pros first and trickles down later. But the direction is set: the machine on your desk is becoming an AI computer in its own right, not a terminal for someone else's. Build for that machine, and you build for where the market is going. Sources: Reuters (October 27, 2026); PYMNTS coverage of the announcement. Figures are Apple's claims as reported; independent benchmarks pending.

articles.title: Micro-Fluidic Dynamics in Vertical Robotics: Ultrasonic Atomization, Piezoelectric Pumps, and Thermal Dissipation
articles.description: Automating floor cleaning involves relatively generous payload tolerances; carrying a 300ml water reservoir and passive drip wicks is mechanically trivial. Vertical glass-cleaning robotics, however, operate under severe mass constraints. Every added gram of cleaning fluid increases motor torque demands and dynamic slip risk. To achieve streak-free optical clarity without saturating the microfiber tracks, high-end vertical platforms rely on ultrasonic atomization and active fluid metering. Here is a technical breakdown of how micro-fluidic delivery and thermal dissipation operate under high-load vertical conditions. Piezoelectric Atomization and Droplet Sizing Passive gravity feeds or standard mechanical sprayers fail on vertical glass: excessive droplet volume causes immediate run-off streaks before the scrubbing pads can make contact. Modern systems integrate piezoelectric ceramic transducer discs vibrating at ultrasonic frequencies (typically between 108 kHz and 115 kHz): The high-frequency oscillation breaks surface tension, converting cleaning solution into a dense aerosol mist with uniform droplet diameters between 10 and 15 micrometers. Precise droplet sizing ensures the mist remains suspended long enough to adhere evenly to the pane without pooling or dripping downward due to gravity. Micro-solenoid valves or micro-peristaltic pumps deliver sub-milliliter pulses (approximately 0.1ml per burst) synchronized precisely with the robot’s advance cadence. Liquid Viscosity and Surface Tension Dynamics Not all cleaning agents behave identically at the micro-nozzle interface: High-purity deionized water provides consistent cavitation but lacks surfactant action to break down organic window grime. Commercial alcohol-based or surfactant solutions lower surface tension, improving soil encapsulation, but their rapid evaporation rates alter pad friction dynamics over long cycles. The embedded controller must calibrate spray intervals against ambient relative humidity and temperature. If surface friction drops below 0.35, the drive wheels register micro-slippage via optical rotary encoders, prompting an immediate reduction in spray duty cycle. Thermal Dissipation in Hermetically Sealed Vacuum Chambers Operating a brushless centrifugal turbine at 25,000 RPM inside a compact, weather-sealed chassis generates substantial thermal buildup. Because the suction enclosure must maintain negative pressure (-3.5 kPa to -5.0 kPa), conventional open ventilation is impossible: Stator heat from the primary turbine motor is directed across aluminum heat sinks placed directly in the path of the exhaust airflow. The high-speed exhaust air carries motor heat out through top deflection vents, away from both the glass and the sensitive micro-fluidic reservoirs. Thermal sensors placed near the internal emergency Li-ion battery pack continuously monitor ambient chamber temperatures. If internal temperatures exceed 65 degrees Celsius, thermal throttling reduces motor duty cycles to protect cell chemistry. Empirical Benchmarks and Mechanical Telemetry Achieving optimal micro-spray coverage without clogging requires extensive stress testing across varying water hardness levels and continuous runtime stress cycles. Critical lab benchmarks include: Long-term nozzle orifice degradation and calcification rates under non-distilled water usage. Thermal imaging profiles under continuous 90-minute multi-pane operation. Dynamic friction variation before and after micro-spray dispersion on heavy-gauge tempered glass. For detailed hardware teardowns, ultrasonic spray flow-rate evaluations, and comprehensive lab benchmark datasets across commercial platforms, review the empirical engineering reports published at Window Robot Lab:https://windowrobotlab.com/ Have you worked with ultrasonic atomizers or micro-fluidic dosing in embedded hardware? How do you prevent nozzle calcification and handle thermal dissipation in enclosed chassis? Share your insights and schematics in the comments below.

articles.title: PostgreSQL 19 - Monitoring Lock Contention and Fast-Path Overflow with pg_stat_lock
articles.description: PostgreSQL 19 introduces the pg_stat_lock view, which provides cumulative statistics about lock activity across the database cluster. It helps database administrators investigate lock contention, measure time spent waiting for locks, and identify situations where relation locks exceed the available fast-path slots. In this article, I will demonstrate these capabilities through two practical scenarios. postgres=# \d pg_stat_lock View "pg_catalog.pg_stat_lock" Column | Type | Collation | Nullable | Default -------------------+--------------------------+-----------+----------+--------- locktype | text | | | waits | bigint | | | wait_time | double precision | | | fastpath_exceeded | bigint | | | stats_reset | timestamp with time zone | | | The view contains the following columns: locktype: Type of lockable object, such as a relation or transaction ID waits: Number of qualifying lock waits wait_time: Total time spent waiting for locks, in milliseconds fastpath_exceeded: Number of times a lock could not be acquired through the fast path because the available slots were exceeded stats_reset: Time when the statistics were last reset Initially, all counters are zero in my test environment. The view returns 12 rows, one for each lock type. postgres=# SELECT * FROM pg_stat_lock; locktype | waits | wait_time | fastpath_exceeded | stats_reset ------------------+-------+-----------+-------------------+------------------------------- relation | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 extend | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 frozenid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 page | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 tuple | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 transactionid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 virtualxid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 spectoken | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 object | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 userlock | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 advisory | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 applytransaction | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 (12 rows) An important detail is that waits and wait_time only include waits that exceed deadlock_timeout and end with successful lock acquisition. In my environment, the configured threshold is one second: vahiddb=# SHOW deadlock_timeout; deadlock_timeout ------------------ 1s (1 row) Investigating Lock Waits In this scenario, I will demonstrate how pg_stat_lock records lock waits caused by concurrent transactions. Concurrent Updates I will use an existing table named tbl_counter. The table contains a counter row that both sessions attempt to update. Before starting the experiment, I reset the lock statistics: vahiddb=# SELECT pg_stat_reset_shared('lock'); pg_stat_reset_shared ---------------------- Session 1 Start a transaction and update the counter: --session 1: vahiddb=# begin; update tbl_counter set counter=counter+1; BEGIN UPDATE 1 The update completes, but the transaction remains open. PostgreSQL retains the relevant locks until the transaction ends. Session 2 While Session 1 remains open, execute the same update: --session 2: vahiddb=# update tbl_counter set counter=counter+1; The second update waits because Session 1 has modified the same row and has not yet committed. At this point, querying pg_stat_lock shows that the counters have not increased for this wait: vahiddb=# SELECT * FROM pg_stat_lock; The waits and wait_time values remain zero in the displayed statistics. Why? The second transaction is still waiting. PostgreSQL records this qualifying wait in the cumulative statistics when the lock is successfully acquired after the wait ends, rather than incrementing the counters continuously while the transaction is blocked. Commit the first transaction: vahiddb=*# commit; COMMIT Session 2 can now proceed and complete its update. Query the statistics again: ------------------+-------+------------+-------------------+------------------------------- transactionid | 1 | 332098.097 | 0 | 2026-10-26 08:56:30.602553+03 The recorded wait_time is approximately 332 seconds. The important observation is that the wait was recorded under transactionid, rather than relation. Although both sessions executed an UPDATE against the same table, the second transaction waited for the transaction ID of the transaction holding the conflicting row lock. This illustrates why the locktype column is useful: it identifies the type of lockable object associated with the recorded wait, rather than simply naming the SQL operation that caused it. Table-Level Lock Contention Now let's generate a wait involving a relation lock. First, reset the statistics again: Acquire an exclusive table lock and keep the transaction open: LOCK TABLE tbl_counter IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE; LOCK TABLE The ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock conflicts with the ACCESS SHARE lock required by a normal SELECT. While Session 1 holds the lock, execute: vahiddb=# select * from tbl_counter; The query waits until Session 1 releases its lock. Commit the transaction: After Session 2 completes, query the statistics: relation | 1 | 63338.103 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 extend | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 frozenid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 page | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 tuple | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 transactionid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 virtualxid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 spectoken | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 object | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 userlock | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 advisory | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 applytransaction | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 09:34:16.935286+03 The relation row records one qualifying wait, with approximately 63.3 seconds of accumulated wait time. This example differs from the concurrent-update scenario. The ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock directly prevents another session from acquiring the relation lock required by its SELECT statement. Consequently, the recorded wait appears under relation. The wait duration depends on the actual time the second session spends waiting. PostgreSQL only includes waits exceeding deadlock_timeout that subsequently end in successful acquisition. Detecting Fast-Path Lock Overflow PostgreSQL uses a fast-path mechanism to acquire certain relation locks efficiently. When the available fast-path slots are insufficient for a backend's relation-lock requirements, additional lock acquisitions can use the regular shared lock table instead. The fastpath_exceeded counter helps identify this activity. Unlike waits and wait_time, it does not depend on a lock wait exceeding deadlock_timeout. This is particularly interesting for partition-heavy workloads, where a single query can access thousands of relations. First, check the current value of max_locks_per_transaction: vahiddb=# SHOW max_locks_per_transaction; max_locks_per_transaction --------------------------- 128 This setting helps determine the capacity used for lock management. It is not a direct limit on the total number of locks a transaction can acquire, and the fast-path slot limit should not be interpreted as simply being identical to this value. To generate a workload that accesses many relations, I created a range-partitioned table with 5,000 partitions. vahiddb=# CREATE TABLE tbl_parts ( id integer ) PARTITION BY RANGE (id); CREATE TABLE Next, I created the partitions using a DO block: vahiddb=# DO $$ FOR i IN 1..5000 LOOP EXECUTE format( 'CREATE TABLE tbl_parts_%s PARTITION OF tbl_parts FOR VALUES FROM (%s) TO (%s)', i, (i - 1) * 1000, i * 1000 ); END LOOP; END $$; DO Time: 68588.738 ms (01:08.589) The operation completed successfully and took approximately 68.6 seconds in my environment. The table is empty, but its partition structure provides a useful test case because a query against the parent can require locks on many relations. Before executing the test query, I reset the lock statistics: At this stage, the fastpath_exceeded counters were zero. Resetting the statistics makes it easier to attribute subsequent counter changes to the experiment. This function resets cluster-wide lock statistics, so it should be used carefully on shared or production servers. Now, execute a simple aggregate query: vahiddb=# SELECT count(*) FROM tbl_parts; count ------- 0 Although the table contains no rows, PostgreSQL still needs to process the partitioned relation and its partitions. The query therefore provides a way to investigate relation-lock activity without inserting thousands of rows. Next, query pg_stat_lock again: relation | 0 | 0 | 92796 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 extend | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 frozenid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 page | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 tuple | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 transactionid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 virtualxid | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 spectoken | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 object | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 userlock | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 advisory | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 applytransaction | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2026-10-26 10:13:47.582012+03 The fastpath_exceeded counter increased to 92,796. This result shows that the workload generated many relation-lock acquisitions that could not use the fast path because its available slots had been exceeded. Conclusion The pg_stat_lock view in PostgreSQL 19 provides a useful way to investigate lock activity through cumulative statistics.
